\begin{abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in scientific writing~\cite{kobak2024}.
We study whether detectors remain reliable after paraphrasing, reporting an AUROC of 0.91.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Detecting machine-generated text matters for peer review \citep{liang2024,krishna2023}.
Prior work showed that paraphrasing with DIPPER reduces DetectGPT accuracy from 70.3\% to 4.6\%
\citep[see][p.~4]{krishna2023}. % TODO: double-check this number
Our method builds on Fast-DetectGPT~\cite{bao2024} and the transition graph in Fig.~\ref{fig:overview}.

We evaluate on 12,000 abstracts from \textit{arXiv} and \emph{PubMed}, where the
probability $p(x_i \mid x_{<i})$ is computed with GPT-2. Schr\"odinger-style notation is avoided.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{itemize}
  \item A benchmark of human, AI and AI-paraphrased abstracts (Section~\ref{sec:data}).
  \item A detector that is robust to paraphrase attacks:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item statistical features, and
    \item sentence-transition graph features.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{itemize}

\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
The score is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:score}:
\begin{equation}
  S(x) = \frac{\log p(x) - \tilde{\mu}}{\tilde{\sigma}} \label{eq:score}
\end{equation}
where $\tilde{\mu}$ and $\tilde{\sigma}$ are analytic estimates.
\[ B = \frac{\sigma_L - \mu_L}{\sigma_L + \mu_L} \]
